title: Raga Suhi
hook: a raga of union and weddings that opens with a clean vessel, a pot of milk and a churn

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Tilang, sung to Lalo. Your line: truth to power.

A steel pot on the kitchen counter, a dish towel over the lid, left alone for the night. Warm milk went in, then a spoonful of yesterday's yogurt. By morning the two have become one thing, thick and set, and nobody can pull them apart again. Punjabi kitchens know that pot, and so does the Guru Granth Sahib. Today's raga is tied by tradition to weddings and union, and its very first hymn isn't about a bride at all. It's about the pot. Today: Raga Suhi.
screen: `A POT LEFT FOR THE NIGHT.` → `TWO BECOME ONE THING.` → `A RAGA OF UNION OPENS IN A KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Suhi follows Tilang in the Granth's order, opening on ang seven twenty-eight. Sikh tradition links it with union and weddings, and its pages hold songs of the bride and the beloved; tomorrow opens some of them. Second, the kitchen. Guru Nanak's opening hymn, in paraphrase: wash the vessel, sit down, purify it with incense, and only then go out for the milk. The milk is your deeds. Awareness is the culture you stir in. And set it free of craving for a reward. Third, the refrain: chant the one Name; every other work bears no fruit. Fourth, the churn. Make this mind the handles, and staying awake the cord. Let the tongue repeat the Name, and churn like that: this is how the nectar is found. Why would a raga of union begin here? Milk and culture become one only in a clean pot, left in peace, with nobody poking at it to see if it's ready. The hymn describes union the way a cook does: prepare the vessel, bring something good, add a little of what's alive, and wait without grasping. Then the churning, the patient work that brings out what was hidden. Some readers hear the soul and God becoming one. Others hear a plain daily discipline. Both start with the same instruction: wash the pot first. Union.
screen: `SUHI FOLLOWS TILANG.` · `WASH THE VESSEL, THEN FETCH THE MILK.` · `CHANT THE ONE NAME.` · `THE MIND AS THE CHURN'S HANDLES.` · then, large: `UNION.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, play a shabad in Raga Suhi, or simply let the breath slow. For a minute, wash the pot, letting go of whatever is still sloshing around from today, one thing at a time; then leave it be, without checking whether it's working, like milk left to set, with Waheguru as the one word you stir in if you pray, or the breath alone if you don't.
Raga Suhi. The raga after Tilang, linked by tradition with weddings and union, which opens with a clean vessel, milk, a little culture and a churn. Today's word.
Your line: union. A clean pot, left in peace, with something alive stirred in. Day one thousand ninety-four, done.

howItsDone: Shabads from the Suhi section of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan in Raga Suhi, and because Suhi holds the Lavan, the raga is heard at the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding.

what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's first Suhi hymn (ang 728) maps the whole dairy process, washing, setting and churning, onto devotion, with the refrain japahu ta eko nama, chant the one Name.

chat.says: Suhi is a wedding raga, so why does it open with milk and a pot?
options: Union needs a clean vessel left in peace: wash the pot, add good deeds, wait.
It's a recipe the Guru gave for the food served at weddings.
It warns that cooking and chores keep you from thinking of God.
chat.meaning: The hymn: wash the vessel, then fetch the milk of your deeds and stir in awareness. It describes union the way a cook does.

notes: Paraphrase of Suhi Mahalla 1, Ang 728: bhaanda dhoe bais dhoop devhu tau doodhai kau jaavahu; doodh karam phun surat samaain hoe niraas jamaavahu; japahu ta eko nama, avar niraphal kaama (rahao); ihu man eetee haath karahu phun netrau need na aavai; rasna naam japahu tab matheeai, in bidh amrit paavahu. Please confirm the paraphrase, especially 'eetee' (churn handles) and 'netrau' (churning cord).
'Sikh tradition links it with union and weddings' follows the outline; the raga-mood claim is attributed to tradition.
'Punjabi kitchens know that pot' is an everyday description, not a claim about how many.
howItsDone says the Lavan are in Suhi and sung at the Anand Karaj, per the Sikh Rehat Maryada.
